title: Extended Mathematics MYP 5 Full eAssessment Mock

questions.content:
A community garden committee has 60 m of fencing. It will fence a rectangular vegetable plot using the fencing on three sides; the fourth side is an existing brick wall. The side perpendicular to the wall has length x metres.

(a) Show that the area of the plot is A = 60x − 2x² square metres. (2 marks)
(b) The committee wants the plot to have an area of exactly 400 m². Solve an equation to find the two possible values of x, and state the length of the side parallel to the wall in each case. (3 marks)
(c) Write A in the form A = a(x − h)² + k and hence state the largest possible area and the value of x that gives it. (3 marks)
(d) Seed packets are only sold for plots of at least 432 m². Determine the range of values of x for which A ≥ 432. (2 marks)

Total for Question 1: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Length parallel to wall = 60 − 2x
[1] A = x(60 − 2x) = 60x − 2x² (must be shown, not just stated)
(b)
[1] 60x − 2x² = 400 → 2x² − 60x + 400 = 0 → x² − 30x + 200 = 0
[1] (x − 10)(x − 20) = 0 → x = 10 or x = 20
[1] Parallel side: 60 − 20 = 40 m when x = 10; 60 − 40 = 20 m when x = 20
(c)
[1] Method: factor out −2 and complete the square: A = −2(x² − 30x) = −2[(x − 15)² − 225]
[1] A = −2(x − 15)² + 450
[1] Largest area 450 m² when x = 15 m. ECF from the completed-square form.
(d)
[1] Method: 2x² − 60x + 432 ≤ 0 → x² − 30x + 216 ≤ 0 → (x − 12)(x − 18) ≤ 0
[1] 12 ≤ x ≤ 18
Common errors: forgetting to halve the 60 − 2x relationship (using 60 − x); giving only x-values in (b) and not the parallel lengths; reversing the inequality sign in (d).

questions.content:
A footbridge over a canal has a parabolic arch. Taking the left foot of the arch as the origin, the height of the arch above the water level is modelled by y = 0.8x − 0.02x², where x is the horizontal distance in metres from the left foot and y is the height in metres. Both are measured on level ground at water level.

(a) Show that the span of the arch (the horizontal distance between its two feet) is 40 m. (2 marks)
(b) Determine the maximum height of the arch and the value of x where it occurs. (2 marks)
(c) A surveyor measures the actual height of the arch at x = 5 m and records 3.8 m. Calculate the percentage error of the model's prediction at x = 5 m. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (2 marks)
(d) A vertical support cable is attached to the arch at a height of 6 m. Find the two possible horizontal positions of the cable. (3 marks)
(e) A barge 12 m wide must pass under the arch, centred under its highest point. The barge carries a cabin whose top is 7.5 m above the water. Use the model to determine whether the barge can pass through without touching the arch. (2 marks)
(f) State one limitation of using this model to decide whether the barge can pass. (1 mark)

Total for Question 2: 12 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Set y = 0: 0.8x − 0.02x² = 0 → x(0.8 − 0.02x) = 0
[1] x = 0 or x = 40, so span = 40 m
(b)
[1] Axis of symmetry halfway between roots: x = 20
[1] y = 0.8(20) − 0.02(400) = 16 − 8 = 8 m maximum height. Accept completing the square.
(c)
[1] Model value: 0.8(5) − 0.02(25) = 3.5 m
[1] Percentage error = |3.5 − 3.8| ÷ 3.8 × 100 = 7.9% (7.89...%). Using 3.5 as the denominator gives 8.6%: award one mark only for correct method with the wrong denominator.
(d)
[1] 0.8x − 0.02x² = 6 → 0.02x² − 0.8x + 6 = 0 → x² − 40x + 300 = 0
[1] (x − 10)(x − 30) = 0
[1] x = 10 m and x = 30 m from the left foot (symmetry about x = 20 supports the answer)
(e)
[1] Barge occupies x = 14 to x = 26; the arch is lowest at its edges: y(14) = 11.2 − 3.92 = 7.28 m
[1] 7.28 < 7.5 so the cabin would touch the arch: the barge cannot pass. Accept y(26) = 7.28 by symmetry.
(f)
[1] Any one valid limitation, e.g. the water level changes with weather or lock operation; the real arch has thickness so the underside is lower than the modelled line; the model ignores the barge's pitching or a safety clearance; the model is only a rounded curve of the real arch.
Common errors: using the maximum height 8 m as the clearance (ignores the barge width); using x = 6 and x = 34 instead of 14 and 26.

questions.content:
A hospital uses a drug whose concentration in a patient's blood decreases over time. After an injection, the concentration is modelled by C = 120 × 0.8^t, where C is in mg per litre and t is the time in hours after the injection.

(a) Calculate the concentration 3 hours after the injection. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (2 marks)
(b) State the percentage by which the concentration decreases each hour. (1 mark)
(c) The drug is only effective while the concentration is at least 30 mg per litre. Use logarithms to determine how long the drug stays effective. Give your answer in hours to 2 decimal places. (3 marks)
(d) The half-life is the time taken for the concentration to fall to half of its starting value. Calculate the half-life of the drug to 2 decimal places. (2 marks)
(e) A nurse measures the concentration 2 hours after injection and records 80 mg per litre. Calculate the percentage error of the model's prediction at t = 2, taking the nurse's reading as the true value. (2 marks)
(f) A doctor wants to use the model to schedule doses over the next 12 hours. Justify whether this is reasonable, referring to one assumption of the model. (2 marks)

Total for Question 3: 12 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: 120 × 0.8³
[1] 61.4 mg per litre (61.44)
(b)
[1] 20% decrease each hour (1 − 0.8 = 0.2)
(c)
[1] Set 120 × 0.8^t = 30 → 0.8^t = 0.25
[1] t = log 0.25 ÷ log 0.8 (any base, or ln)
[1] t = 6.21 hours (6.2126...). Accept trial and improvement only with the final answer correct to 2 decimal places, award two marks maximum otherwise.
(d)
[1] 0.8^t = 0.5
[1] t = log 0.5 ÷ log 0.8 = 3.11 hours (3.106...)
(e)
[1] Model value 120 × 0.8² = 76.8 mg per litre
[1] Percentage error = (80 − 76.8) ÷ 80 × 100 = 4.0%
(f)
[1] Valid judgement with reason, e.g. model predicts the concentration only changes by a constant percentage so it never reaches zero; it assumes no further doses, a single injection and a constant rate of removal in every patient
[1] Conclusion linked to the reason: e.g. reasonable for estimating the time until the drug falls below 30 mg per litre (about 6.2 hours) but doses after that need new measurements because the model assumes one injection only and patient kidney function varies. Accept any consistent justified view.
Common errors: using 0.2^t as the base; dividing by 30 instead of 120; confusing half-life with the time to reach 30.

questions.content:
A designer creates a series of patterns using square tiles. Pattern n has a square of n × n grey tiles surrounded by a single-width border of white tiles.

Pattern 1: 1 grey tile, border of 8 white tiles
Pattern 2: 4 grey tiles, border of 12 white tiles
Pattern 3: 9 grey tiles, border of 16 white tiles

(a) Pattern 4 follows the same rule. Write down the number of grey tiles and the number of white tiles in Pattern 4. (2 marks)
(b) Find a general rule, in terms of n, for the number of white tiles in Pattern n. (2 marks)
(c) Test your rule by predicting the number of white tiles in Pattern 10, and then verify your prediction by counting the total number of tiles in a 12 × 12 square and subtracting the grey tiles. (3 marks)
(d) Show algebraically that the number of white tiles equals (n + 2)² − n² and that this simplifies to your rule in (b). (2 marks)
(e) Investigate whether there is a pattern in which the number of grey tiles equals the number of white tiles. Justify your conclusion. (3 marks)
(f) Prove that the number of grey tiles in Pattern (n + 1) is always exactly 2n + 1 more than in Pattern n, and hence justify that the difference is always an odd number. (2 marks)

Total for Question 4: 14 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Grey tiles = 16
[1] White tiles = 20
(b)
[1] Recognises the white tiles form an arithmetic sequence 8, 12, 16, 20 with common difference 4
[1] White = 4n + 4 (accept 4(n + 1))
(c)
[1] Prediction: 4(10) + 4 = 44 white tiles
[1] Total tiles in Pattern 10 = 12 × 12 = 144
[1] 144 − 100 = 44, which matches the prediction, so the rule is verified
(d)
[1] Total tiles (n + 2)² = n² + 4n + 4, so white = (n + 2)² − n²
[1] = n² + 4n + 4 − n² = 4n + 4
(e)
[1] Set n² = 4n + 4 → n² − 4n − 4 = 0
[1] n = (4 ± √32) ÷ 2 = 2 ± 2√2, so n = 4.83 (positive root)
[1] Not a whole number, so no pattern has equal grey and white tiles (Pattern 4 has 16 grey and 20 white, Pattern 5 has 25 grey and 24 white, so the counts cross between them but never match). Accept a table of values showing the crossing and a conclusion.
(f)
[1] (n + 1)² − n² = n² + 2n + 1 − n² = 2n + 1
[1] 2n + 1 is 2 × a whole number plus 1, so it is odd for every whole number n
Common errors: writing 4n instead of 4n + 4 (forgetting the corners); testing the rule only on the given cases; stating "no solution" without evidence.

questions.content:
A ship leaves port P and sails 14 km on a bearing of 060° to a buoy Q. It then turns and sails 9 km on a bearing of 150° to a second buoy R. A lighthouse L stands 20 km from P on a bearing of 110°.

(a) Show that angle PQR = 90°. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the direct distance PR. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the bearing of R from P, to the nearest 0.1 of a degree. (3 marks)
(d) Use the cosine rule to calculate the distance LR. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (3 marks)
(e) Calculate the area of triangle PLR. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)

Total for Question 5: 12 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Bearing of P from Q = 060° + 180° = 240°
[1] Angle between QP (240°) and QR (150°) = 240° − 150° = 90°. Accept alternate-angle reasoning from a north line at Q.
(b)
[1] Method: Pythagoras PR² = 14² + 9² = 277
[1] PR = 16.6 km (16.643...)
(c)
[1] Method: angle QPR = tan⁻¹(9 ÷ 14)
[1] Angle QPR = 32.7° (32.735...)
[1] Bearing = 060° + 32.7° = 092.7°. ECF for a correct method with a wrong angle.
(d)
[1] Angle RPL = 110° − 92.7° = 17.3° (17.26... unrounded)
[1] Method: LR² = 16.6² + 20² − 2 × 16.6 × 20 × cos 17.3°
[1] LR = 6.4 km (6.42...). Accept 6.4 to 6.5 depending on rounding. ECF from (b) and (c).
(e)
[1] Method: area = ½ × 16.6 × 20 × sin 17.3°
[1] 49.4 km² (49.395...). ECF from (d); accept 49.3 to 49.5.
Common errors: measuring bearings from the wrong north line; forgetting that bearings are three figures; using the sine rule when the included angle is known.

questions.content:
A water tank is made from a cylinder topped with a hemisphere of the same radius. The cylinder has radius 1.5 m and height 2.4 m. The base is on the ground and is not painted.

(a) Calculate the volume of the cylindrical part. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the volume of the hemispherical part. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)
(c) The tank is completely full. Given that 1 m³ = 1000 litres, calculate the number of litres of water in the tank to the nearest 100 litres. (1 mark)
(d) Calculate the total outside surface area to be painted (curved cylinder surface and hemisphere). Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (3 marks)
(e) A circular pipe of radius 0.5 m is connected to the tank. A flat plate (a chord of the circular cross-section) is 0.8 m long. Calculate the perpendicular distance from the centre of the circle to the chord. (2 marks)
(f) Points A, B and C lie on a circle and AC is a diameter. Angle BAC = 35°. Calculate angle ACB and name the circle theorem you used. (2 marks)

Total for Question 6: 12 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: π × 1.5² × 2.4
[1] 17.0 m³ (16.96...)
(b)
[1] Method: ⅔ × π × 1.5³ (or half of 4/3 π r³)
[1] 7.07 m³ (7.068...)
(c)
[1] 24.03 m³ = 24 000 litres to the nearest 100 litres (accept 24 000)
(d)
[1] Curved cylinder surface: 2 × π × 1.5 × 2.4 = 22.6 m²
[1] Hemisphere: 2 × π × 1.5² = 14.1 m²
[1] Total = 36.8 m² (36.76...). Common error: adding the circular base (gives 43.8 m²).
(e)
[1] Half chord = 0.4 m, right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 0.5 m (the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord)
[1] d = √(0.5² − 0.4²) = 0.3 m
(f)
[1] Angle ABC = 90° (angle in a semicircle) so angle ACB = 180° − 90° − 35° = 55°
[1] Names the theorem: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle
Common errors: using diameter instead of radius; forgetting the 1/2 for the hemisphere; adding the flat top circle that does not exist.

questions.content:
A school surveys 80 students about their journey times to school, t minutes.

Time t (minutes):   0 < t ≤ 10 | 10 < t ≤ 20 | 20 < t ≤ 30 | 30 < t ≤ 40 | 40 < t ≤ 60
Frequency:                8            22            26            16            8

(a) Complete the cumulative frequency column for these five classes. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate an estimate of the mean journey time. (3 marks)
(c) Use the cumulative frequencies and linear interpolation within the median class to estimate the median. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (2 marks)

The same school records the weekly study time x (hours) and the test score y (%) of six students:

x: 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10
y: 48, 55, 58, 66, 71, 80

(d) Find the equation of the line of best fit for y in terms of x, and interpret the gradient in this context. (3 marks)
(e) Use your line to predict the score for a student who studies 6 hours. Then explain why the line should not be used to predict the score for a student who studies 25 hours. (2 marks)

Total for Question 7: 12 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Cumulative frequencies 8, 30, 56 (first three)
[1] 72, 80 (last two)
(b)
[1] Midpoints 5, 15, 25, 35, 50
[1] Sum of f × midpoint = 40 + 330 + 650 + 560 + 400 = 1980
[1] Mean = 1980 ÷ 80 = 24.75, so about 24.8 minutes
(c)
[1] Median is the 40th value, in the class 20 < t ≤ 30 (cumulative frequency 30 before it)
[1] 20 + (40 − 30) ÷ 26 × 10 = 23.8 minutes (23.85...; accept 23.8 or 23.9)
(d)
[1] Gradient = 4 (method: regression on a calculator or gradient from means (6, 63))
[1] y = 4x + 39
[1] Interpretation: each extra hour of weekly study is associated with 4 more percentage points in the test score (correlation, not proof of cause)
(e)
[1] 4(6) + 39 = 63%
[1] x = 25 gives 139%, which is impossible (score cannot exceed 100%); this is extrapolation far outside the data range of 2 to 10 hours.
Common errors: using class boundaries instead of midpoints; dividing by 5 instead of 80; claiming study causes the score without qualification; ignoring the context in (e).

questions.content:
A factory has two machines making bolts. Machine A makes 60% of the bolts and Machine B makes the other 40%. Of the bolts made by Machine A, 3% are defective. Of the bolts made by Machine B, 5% are defective.

(a) A bolt is chosen at random. Calculate the probability that it is defective. You may use a tree diagram. (3 marks)
(b) A randomly chosen bolt is found to be defective. Calculate the probability that it came from Machine B. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (3 marks)
(c) A box is filled with 3 bolts, all from Machine A. Calculate the probability that at least one bolt in the box is defective. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)
(d) The factory ships 5000 bolts. The contract allows a penalty-free defect rate of at most 4%. Calculate the expected number of defective bolts and justify whether the factory is expected to meet the contract. (2 marks)

Total for Question 8: 10 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] P(A and defective) = 0.6 × 0.03 = 0.018
[1] P(B and defective) = 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.02
[1] P(defective) = 0.018 + 0.02 = 0.038
(b)
[1] Conditional probability method: P(B | defective) = P(B and defective) ÷ P(defective)
[1] = 0.02 ÷ 0.038. ECF from (a).
[1] = 0.526 (0.5263...)
(c)
[1] Method: 1 − 0.97³ (complement of no defective)
[1] 0.0873 (0.087327)
(d)
[1] Expected defective = 0.038 × 5000 = 190
[1] 190 ÷ 5000 = 3.8% which is below 4%, so the factory is expected to meet the contract; the expected value is an average, so in an actual shipment the number could exceed 200 by chance. Award for a conclusion linked to the figures.
Common errors: adding 0.03 and 0.05 directly; giving 0.02 ÷ 0.4 in (b); treating the bolts in (c) as needing exactly one defective.

questions.content:
A town of 12 000 MWh annual electricity demand plans a small wind farm. Each turbine has a rated power of 2.5 MW and, on average, produces electricity at 30% of its rated power for all 8760 hours in a year. The town's demand is expected to increase by 3% every year. Each turbine costs £3.2 million, the connection to the grid costs £0.9 million, and the wind farm costs £0.1 million per year to maintain. The town currently pays £90 per MWh for grid electricity. The council proposes to build two turbines.

(a) Calculate the annual energy output of one turbine in MWh. (2 marks)
(b) Show that two turbines produce more than the town's current annual demand. (1 mark)
(c) Determine, using a suitable model for the demand, the first year in which the annual demand exceeds the output of two turbines. (3 marks)
(d) Assume the wind farm replaces 12 000 MWh of grid electricity each year at £90 per MWh. Calculate the number of years needed for the savings, after maintenance costs, to repay the total construction cost. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (3 marks)
(e) After a year of operation, the measured output of one turbine is 6000 MWh. Calculate the percentage error of the model's prediction for one turbine, taking the measured value as the true value. (2 marks)
(f) Using the measured output, determine in which year demand first exceeds the output of two turbines. Hence evaluate whether building only two turbines is a sustainable plan, and state one assumption or limitation in your calculation. (3 marks)

Total for Question 9: 14 marks
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: 2.5 × 0.30 × 8760
[1] 6570 MWh
(b)
[1] 2 × 6570 = 13 140 MWh, which is greater than 12 000 MWh
(c)
[1] Demand model D = 12 000 × 1.03^n (geometric growth, n years from now)
[1] n = 3: 13 112.7 (below 13 140); n = 4: 13 506.1 (above 13 140). Accept solving 1.03^n > 1.095 with logarithms (n > 3.07).
[1] First year in which demand exceeds output: year 4. ECF from (a).
(d)
[1] Construction cost = 2 × 3.2 + 0.9 = £7.3 million
[1] Annual saving after maintenance = 12 000 × 90 − 100 000 = £980 000
[1] 7 300 000 ÷ 980 000 = 7.4 years (7.449...)
(e)
[1] Model prediction per turbine 6570 versus measured 6000: difference 570
[1] Percentage error = 570 ÷ 6000 × 100 = 9.5%
(f)
[1] Measured output of two turbines = 12 000 MWh; demand after 1 year = 12 360 MWh, which already exceeds it, so the shortfall begins in year 1
[1] Evaluation linked to the numbers, e.g. two turbines do not meet current demand once demand grows, so the plan is not sustainable for the 7.4-year payback; a third turbine (or storage) would be needed. Accept any consistent evaluation.
[1] One valid assumption or limitation, e.g. wind speed varies year to year, a single year of measurement is not representative, the 3% growth may not continue, electricity prices may change, savings do not include turbine lifetime or decommissioning cost.
Common errors: forgetting the grid connection in the cost; forgetting maintenance; using 5% for the growth factor; computing percentage error against the model value instead of the measured value.
